notes.meaning: King Hezekiah invited everyone, both his own people in Judah and the northern tribes of Israel, to keep the Passover at God's temple in Jerusalem. Passover was the yearly feast remembering how God brought Israel out of Egypt. "Ephraim and Manasseh" were the two leading northern tribes, so the names stand for the whole north. Hezekiah's aim was not to win the north back to his throne but to bring the people back to God. He did this even though the north had often troubled Judah, repaying evil with good.

Passover was supposed to be kept in the first month. That year it could not be, because too few priests had been consecrated (set apart and made ready for God's service) and the people had not yet gathered. God's law allowed a person who was unclean or far away to keep Passover a month later (Numbers 9:10-11). Hezekiah and his leaders applied that rule to the whole nation. Rather than wait a whole year and let people's zeal cool, they chose the second month.

The plan pleased the king and all the people. It had two parts: keeping Passover in the second month and inviting the north. King and people were of one mind. Matthew Henry says it is good to strike while the iron is hot and to act while people are eager.

They sent the call through the whole land. "From Beersheba to Dan" means from the far south to the far north. The people had not been keeping Passover together as a whole nation, the way God's law said. Since the kingdom split, this great feast had been badly neglected.

Swift runners, perhaps from the king's guard, carried the letters. The message was simple: turn back to the Lord, and He will turn back to you. He is the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, who made a covenant (a binding promise) with their first fathers. The people being called were a "remnant," the few left after Assyrian kings had already carried many away.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think this Passover came a few years later, after the northern kingdom had already fallen to Assyria. On that view, the letter spoke to survivors left in a ruined land.

notes.meaning: Hezekiah pointed to what had happened to their fathers and brothers. They had been unfaithful to God, and they were ruined and carried off, as everyone could see. Matthew Henry puts it this way: let their harms be your warnings.

"Stiffen your necks" means being stubborn, like an ox that won't bow to the yoke. "Submit to the LORD" is literally "give the hand," like shaking hands to seal a promise. It means agreeing to take God as your God and to stop resisting Him. Then they were to come to His temple and serve Him, so His anger would turn away. Matthew Henry says we all inherit this stubbornness, and it must be overcome.

The letter ends with hope. If they returned to God, even their captured family members might find mercy and come home. God is gracious and merciful and will not turn His face away from those who come back. If we return to God in obedience, He will return to us in mercy. God's rich mercy is the strongest reason to repent (turn from sin back to God).

Most people in the north laughed at the messengers and mocked them. After so long away from God, they had lost their hunger for His worship. Matthew Henry and Wesley note that the northern kingdom was carried into captivity soon after. Turning down this offer of grace left them without excuse. Still, the Geneva Notes say that even when people mock, God's word keeps working in the hearts of His own.

Even so, some from Asher, Manasseh and Zebulun humbled themselves and came. To humble themselves means they were sorry for their sins and gave in to God. In the worst of times God always has a remnant, a faithful few. Pride keeps people from yielding to God. When pride is brought down, the work is done.

In Judah, God's hand was at work for good, not for judgment. He gave the people one heart to obey. Their unity was God's gift, since it is God who works in us both to want and to do what is good. When people are unexpectedly eager to do right, we should see God's hand in it.

differ.view: Some obey God's call and others mock it because God's Spirit moves in the hearts of the first group, while the others are left to themselves.

notes.meaning: A very large crowd gathered in Jerusalem in the second month. They came for the Feast of Unleavened Bread, the week of eating bread made without yeast that follows Passover. This gathering was long remembered as one of the greatest Passovers.

Before the feast, the people tore down the false altars and incense altars that King Ahaz had set up around the city. They threw them into the Kidron Valley. We must put away what offends God before we can worship Him rightly. The best way to prepare for worship is to cast away our sins.

On the fourteenth day they killed the Passover lambs. The priests and Levites (the temple helpers) were ashamed. Ordinary people were more eager to worship than the leaders who should have been first. That shame moved them to get ready and offer the sacrifices. Seeing the zeal of others should make us ashamed of our own coldness and stir us to serve well.

The priests took their places as Moses' law required and sprinkled the blood of the lambs on the altar. Usually each family head killed his own lamb. This time many worshippers were ceremonially unclean, meaning not fit by the law's rules to handle holy things. So the Levites killed the lambs for them, so the sacrifices would not be spoiled. Matthew Henry sees the sprinkled blood as a picture of Christ, our Passover Lamb.

Many from the northern tribes ate the Passover without being made clean, which broke the law's rules. They did it not out of rebellion but out of ignorance, coming from places full of idol worship. Hezekiah prayed that the good Lord would provide atonement (cover their sin so He could forgive) for everyone whose heart was set on seeking Him. A sincere heart counts for more with God than perfect ceremony. Yet Henry warns that nothing makes up for a heart that is not truly seeking God.

God heard Hezekiah's prayer and "healed" the people. That means He forgave their fault and accepted them and their worship as if they had been clean. In the Bible, sin is often pictured as a sickness of the soul, and forgiveness as healing. God's healing also brings comfort and peace.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think "healed" means God kept away the sickness the people feared would come from breaking the purity laws (Leviticus 15:31).

notes.meaning: For seven days the people kept the feast with great joy. Every day the priests and Levites praised God with songs and loud instruments, celebrating His power. Praising God should fill much of our time when we gather to worship.

Hezekiah spoke warm, encouraging words to the Levites who served so well. Older translations say they "taught the good knowledge of the LORD," which Henry and Clarke take as teaching God's Word to the people. The people shared fellowship offerings, which were meals eaten as a sign of peace and friendship with God. They also gave thanks to the God of their fathers. Leaders do much good when they encourage faithful ministers.

The worship was so sweet that the whole crowd chose to stay seven more days. Many were far from home and in the middle of harvest, yet they were in no hurry to leave. Holy things should be done with holy gladness. People who taste joy in God's presence do not quickly tire of it.

Hezekiah and his officials gave thousands of animals so the people could keep feasting. Wesley notes the king's gift was even more generous because his treasury was nearly empty. More priests also made themselves ready, so there were enough hands for the work. Those God has blessed with plenty should gladly use it for His glory.

Everyone rejoiced together: the people of Judah, the priests and Levites, the visitors from the north, and foreigners. Adam Clarke says these foreigners had fully joined the faith of Israel, since only they could eat the Passover. Many of these groups were worshipping side by side for the first time in a long while.

Jerusalem had not seen joy like this since King Solomon dedicated the temple. Since his day the kingdom had been split, and the tribes had never gathered like this for a feast. This feast was like Solomon's in its length, its rich offerings, its crowds and its gladness.

At the end, the priests blessed the people, as God's law told them to do (Numbers 6:23). God heard them, and their prayer reached His home in heaven. God said "Amen" to the blessing. Later blessings, such as Judah's rescue from Assyria, showed that God truly answered.
